conceptTag: Weigh an acquisition offer for an app
readerTitle: A $3 million offer for your app: what is it really worth?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (애견 미용실 예약 앱, 기장 대행 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 인수 제안은 제시된 총액이 아니라 '이 인수자에게 내 회사가 얼마짜리인가'와 '그중 확실히 받는 돈이 얼마인가'라는 두 질문으로 읽는다.
misconception: 인수 제안은 총액이 큰 쪽이 좋은 제안이고, 내 회사의 가치는 내가 버는 이익으로 정해진다.

sources.text: 인수합병의 일반적인 거래 조건 (현금 지급, 주식 지급, 언아웃, 창업자 잔류 조건)

factChecks.note: 앱 제안 구성 계산: 현금 $1.5M + 인수자 주식 $0.9M + 언아웃 $0.6M = $3.0M. 확실한 현금 비중 50%.
기장 대행 회사 제안 계산: 제안 1은 전액 현금 $1.2M, 제안 2는 현금 $0.6M + 언아웃 $0.9M = $1.5M. 제안 2의 확실한 현금은 $0.6M로 제안 1의 절반.
특정 국가의 세금·법률 조언을 피하려고 '거래 구조에 따라 세금이 달라질 수 있으니 전문가와 상의하라'는 일반적인 문장만 넣었습니다. 게시 전 표현을 확인하세요.

cards.title: A $3 million offer for your app
body: Priya built a booking app for dog groomers. About 1,200 salons pay for it each month. It brings in roughly $600,000 a year and keeps about $250,000 after costs.
On a Tuesday morning, an email arrives from a larger company that sells payment software to pet businesses. The subject line: **"Offer to acquire, $3,000,000."**

image.label: A laptop showing an email with a large offer amount
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 작업실 책상 위 노트북 화면에 "Offer to acquire: $3,000,000" 메일. 옆에 강아지 미용 가위와 커피잔. 실제 회사 로고나 메일 서비스 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Priya compare $3 million against?
body: The buyer explains its plan: offer its payment service to every salon on Priya's app.
Before replying, Priya wants a yardstick. Which one matters most?

options.text: What the app earns her on its own each year
options.feedback: This is her walk-away point: below it, keeping the app may be better. But it says nothing about how much this buyer could afford to pay.

options.text: What the buyer can earn from her 1,200 salons once it owns them
options.feedback: This is **what your company is worth to a buyer**. The buyer is paying for its own plan, not just her profit, and that sets how high it can go.

options.text: The price a founder friend got for her app last year
options.feedback: Easy to find, but a different app with a different buyer. It can anchor her far too low or far too high.

cards.title: Her salons are worth more to them than to her.
body: On her own, Priya earns from subscriptions. The buyer could earn from subscriptions *and* from every payment a salon takes, for years.
She can't see the buyer's spreadsheet, but she can estimate the gap. That gap between her value and theirs is the room to negotiate.
It also tells her who else to call. Any company that sells to pet businesses might want the same salons. A second interested buyer is the strongest reason for the first to pay more.

cards.title: Only half of the $3 million is certain.
body: The headline is one number. The offer is really three, and only the first lands in her bank account on signing day.

breakdown.label: Cash at closing
breakdown.detail: Paid when the deal is signed

breakdown.label: Buyer's stock
breakdown.detail: Worth whatever their shares are worth later

breakdown.label: Earnout
breakdown.detail: Paid only if app revenue hits a target in 2 years

breakdown.label: Headline price
breakdown.detail: Plus: Priya must stay for 2 years

cards.softwareNote: Earnouts and stock are common in software deals because buyers are unsure the users will stay after the sale. That risk moves from the buyer to the founder.

cards.title: Priya can push on one thing. Which?
body: Her goal: pay off her house and fund her next project. She plans to stay the two years either way.

options.text: Ask for $3.5M with the same split
options.feedback: A bigger headline feels like a win, but most of the extra would sit in stock and earnout. She'd gain on paper and add risk.

options.text: Accept a lower total, around $2.8M, if more is cash at closing
options.feedback: She trades some upside for certainty, which fits her goal. **Being acquired** means judging the terms, not just the total.

options.text: Accept as is; she'll work hard and hit the earnout
options.feedback: Hard work helps, but after the sale the buyer controls pricing, budget and staff. Effort alone may not hit the target.

cards.title: After signing, it's their company.
body: Priya's earnout depends on app revenue. Yet the buyer plans to bundle her app with payments, maybe at a discount. That could help the buyer and still shrink *her* revenue number.
So before she signs, she asks three questions. Who sets prices? Can they cut her team? How exactly is the target measured?
If the answers put the target out of her hands, that $0.6M deserves little weight when she compares offers.

image.label: Founder handing car keys to a new driver
image.brief: 클레이 일러스트. 창업자가 작은 차의 열쇠를 큰 회사 직원에게 건네고, 차 계기판에 "Earnout target" 게이지. 운전대는 이제 새 주인이 잡고 있다는 느낌. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Don't chase every last dollar of their value.
body: No buyer will hand over all the value its plan might create. It is taking the risk that the plan fails. Pushing too hard can end the talks.
Stock can also fall, and terms that look equal can be taxed very differently depending on where you live. Get a lawyer and an accountant before signing.
And money isn't the only term. Two years working for someone else is part of the price too.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: Marco's firm does the books for 80 small businesses. Two offers arrive. A private investor offers **$1.2M, all cash**. A larger accounting firm offers **$1.5M**: $0.6M cash and $0.9M if clients stay for three years. That firm plans to move clients to its own office and raise fees.

options.text: Take the $1.5M. It's the bigger number
options.feedback: Only $0.6M is certain, and the buyer's own fee increase could drive clients away and cut the earnout.

options.text: Take the $1.2M in cash and move on
options.feedback: Safe and certain. But the larger firm can likely earn more from his clients, so he may be leaving money on the table.

options.text: Go back to the larger firm and ask for more cash at closing
options.feedback: His clients are worth most to the firm that can serve them at scale, and its fee plan threatens the earnout. Use the cash offer as leverage.

cards.title: Ask what you're worth to them, then count what's certain.
body: This lesson used two ideas: **what your company is worth to a buyer** sets how high an offer can go, and the terms of **being acquired** decide how much of that number you actually receive.
**Try it today:** list three companies that could earn more from your customers than you do. Write one sentence on why.
